guide.title: Read this as a state-locality and contention-design case—not as proof that MySQL always beats Redis.
guide.problem: Shopify kept short-lived inventory reservations in Redis while the authoritative inventory ledger lived in MySQL. Reserve operations were fast, but claiming a paid order required changes in two stores without one ACID boundary; the counter also lacked multi-location semantics and imposed a separate cluster's operating cost.
guide.core_idea: Move reservations beside the ledger and replace one hot quantity row with a bounded pool of rows representing reservable units. SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED lets concurrent checkouts acquire different rows; inline replenishment, READ COMMITTED isolation, a composite primary key and consistent lock ordering address the edge cases created by that model.
guide.outcome: Shopify reported meeting its 2025 peak targets after also finding the real throughput ceiling in database-connection usage outside reservation queries. Checkout cleanup removed 50% of primary reads and 33% of primary transactions; during high-volume flash sales, writer CPU stayed below 50% and reader CPU below 16%.
takeaways: Redis was not removed because it was slow. It handled counter concurrency well; the architectural problem was that temporary reservations and the authoritative ledger could not participate in one local transaction, creating oversell and undersell failure windows.

SKIP LOCKED does not make a hot counter parallel. Parallelism came from changing the data model to independently lockable unit rows; SKIP LOCKED then allowed transactions to bypass rows already owned by another checkout.

The 1,000-row cap is workload-derived capacity, not a universal constant. It balances burst absorption against table and scan size and must be recalculated from peak reservation rate, replenishment latency, inventory distribution and database headroom.

Database correctness still required engine-aware work: READ COMMITTED avoided empty-range gap locks, a composite clustered key reduced locks per unit, consistent table ordering removed a deadlock cycle, and UNION ALL reduced cart-level round trips.

Low database CPU did not mean spare end-to-end capacity. Per-caller SQL tags at the application and ProxySQL layers exposed long connection hold times elsewhere in checkout, showing why connection occupancy must be measured alongside query latency and CPU.
review_lenses: Atomicity: which reserve, release, expiry and claim transitions must commit with the ledger, and what invariant survives a crash at every transaction boundary?
Contention: what is the hottest item-location concurrency, how many independently lockable units exist, and what happens when demand exceeds both stock and pool capacity?
Database behavior: verify isolation-level semantics, query plans, lock counts, deadlock retries and empty-pool insertion behavior on the exact MySQL version and schema.
Operations: attribute connection hold time by caller, test shared-database neighbor safety, run shadow comparisons, and preserve an explicit rollback path during gradual cutover.
